# The Magistrate's Garden

In the seventh year of Emperor Xuanzong's reign, Magistrate Wei arrived in the river town of Willow Bend to assume his post. The previous magistrate had died suddenly, leaving behind only whispered rumors and a magnificent garden that the servants refused to enter after dusk.

The garden was indeed extraordinary—moongate passages led through groves of flowering plum trees, and a jade-green pond reflected an elegant pavilion where scholars once composed poetry. But the most remarkable feature was a pear tree of impossible beauty, its blossoms luminous as snow even in autumn, when all other trees stood bare.

On his first evening, Magistrate Wei dismissed the servants' superstitions and took his wine to the pavilion. As the moon rose through the branches, he noticed a young woman in white silk standing beneath the pear tree. Her face was lovely but strange—too pale, as if carved from fine porcelain.

"Forgive my intrusion, Magistrate," she said, her voice like wind through silk. "I am Mei Lian. I've come to warn you."

Before Wei could respond, she vanished like mist.

The next morning, Wei questioned his head servant, Old Chen, who grew pale at the description. "Master, that pear tree..." Chen whispered. "Twenty years ago, a bride named Mei Lian was accused of adultery by her husband's jealous mother. The previous magistrate, eager to curry favor with the powerful family, condemned her without proper evidence. She was buried alive beneath that tree as punishment."

Wei's jaw tightened. "And the previous magistrate?"

"Dead within the month, Master. As was his successor. And the one after that."

That night, Wei returned to the garden despite Chen's pleas. Mei Lian appeared again, more solid this time, her burial robes rustling though no wind stirred.

"You seek justice?" Wei asked.

Her laugh was bitter as winter frost. "Justice? Three magistrates have died in this garden, yet still that tree blooms with unnatural beauty—fed by innocent blood. The family that condemned me grows richer while my bones rest unquiet."

"What would you have me do?"

"What you will," she said. "But know this—every magistrate before you was given the same choice. Investigate my death and risk the wrath of the Zhao family, or ignore it and join me beneath the roots."

Wei spent three days examining dusty scrolls and questioning elderly townspeople who remembered the scandal. The truth emerged like a serpent from tall grass: Mei Lian had refused the advances of her father-in-law. When threatened with exposure, he had conspired with his wife to condemn the innocent bride.

Armed with evidence, Wei could have confronted the Zhao family. They were old now, their patriarch dead, their power waning but still dangerous. Previous magistrates had likely uncovered the same truth and chosen silence over justice.

Instead, Wei did something unexpected.

On the night of the full moon, he brought workers to the garden—not locals, but men from distant provinces who owed him favors. Together, they carefully excavated beneath the pear tree until they found the burial jar containing Mei Lian's remains. Wei personally wrapped the bones in finest silk and arranged for proper funeral rites at the Temple of Merciful Clouds.

The Zhao family, learning of this, arrived in fury. "You dare disturb old graves? We'll have you stripped of rank!"

Wei smiled coldly. "I found evidence of murder while investigating improvements to the official garden. Unless you wish me to reopen a twenty-year-old case with new evidence, you'll sponsor a memorial tablet for Mei Lian and pay for monthly offerings to settle her spirit."

Faced with potential disgrace, the family capitulated.

That final night, Mei Lian appeared one last time in the garden. The terrible pallor had left her face, and she looked almost alive in the moonlight.

"You chose a third path," she said, wonder in her voice. "Neither justice nor injustice, but mercy."

"The dead deserve peace," Wei replied. "And the living deserve the chance to atone. Your death was wrong, but more death would not make it right."

She smiled then, the first warm expression he'd seen from her. "The pear tree will bloom naturally now, beautiful in spring and bare in winter, as nature intended. And you, Magistrate Wei, will live to see your grandchildren play in this garden."

As the first rays of dawn touched the pavilion, Mei Lian faded like morning mist, but this time, Wei knew, she would not return. The garden felt different—still beautiful, but no longer heavy with unspoken sorrow.

Magistrate Wei served in Willow Bend for thirty prosperous years. The pear tree became famous for its spring blossoms, and poets traveled great distances to compose verses beneath its branches. And sometimes, on nights when the moon was especially bright, visitors claimed to smell the faintest fragrance of pear blossoms, even in autumn—not a haunting, but a gentle reminder that justice tempered with mercy can heal even the deepest wounds.
